text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Milne v. Capital Regional District,

2015 BCSC 1163

Date: 20150706

Docket:
14-4240

Registry: Victoria

Between:

Brian
Milne

Plaintiff

And:

Capital
Regional District and Doug McDonald

Defendants

Before: Master Bouck

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

J.
Plonka

Counsel for the Defendant Capital
Regional District:

R.
Bortolin

Counsel for the Defendant/Applicant
D. McDonald:

C.
McDougall

Place and Date of Hearing:

Victoria,
B.C.

June
9, 2015

Place and Date of Judgment:

Victoria,
B.C.

July
6, 2015

The
Application

[
1
]

The defendant McDonald requests an order that various
sections of the amended notice of civil claim (the “NOCC”) be struck pursuant
to Rule 9-5(1)(a) of
Supreme Court Civil Rules
(the “
SCCR
”)
.
As
well, Mr. McDonald seeks particulars on pleas which remain and that such
particulars be incorporated into a further amended notice of civil claim. The
plaintiff says that the application is misconceived as appropriate particulars
have been provided and the other issues raised by the applicant must be decided
at trial. The defendant Capital Regional District (“CRD”) takes no position on
the application.

[
2
]

For reasons which follow, I have concluded that portions
of the NOCC will be struck but no additional particulars need be delivered.

Facts

[
3
]

This is a defamation action. The plaintiff
resides on Saltspring Island on a property adjacent to the local Rod and Gun
Club (the “Club”). This circumstance has been an unhappy one, resulting in four
separate proceedings brought by Mr. Milne in relation to the Club’s
operations. In a petition proceeding, Mr. Milne sought a declaration that the
Club’s operations violated a noise restriction by-law. The CRD sought to amend
its noise control by-law and invited public consultation for that purpose. The
consultation process allowed individuals to submit comments for publication on
the CRD website.

[
4
]

Mr. McDonald submitted the following comment
(reproduced as
verbatim
in the NOCC):

To the CRD
directors, Gentlemen, In regards to the Salt Spring Island Rod and Gun Club,
the Club. It looks to me that we have now come to the very core of the issue,
Milne vs the Club. This issue started whern Mr. Milne first bought his property
next to the club, his mind set then was as it is now, a total shut down of the
club by what ever means available to him. In my opinion he is using the CRD and
the courts. To this end he has befriended and bankrolled the only neighbours
who were complaining about the noise levels. These few neighbours have a long
list of complaints to there credit. Not only do they complain about the
shooting sports but also the noise from sea planes, parties on small craft in
the harbor, Moby’s street dance, extraction fans for the restaurants in Ganges,
the traffic on Ganges hill, cutting the grass at the club and if you care to
check I am sure the CRD has a full list. Wherever Mr Milne buys property there
always seems to be litigation involved until he once again gets his way. This
is like a game to him, buy, litigate and do as he pleases. Has the CRD ever
been informed as to Mr Milne’s final vision for this property or any of
his other holdings on SSI, it would be a safe bet that it is not to be kept as
a working farm. I realize that it is not the CRD’s mandate to “serve and
protect” that falls to the Islands Trust. However this would be an ideal time
for you to check with them and consider the end results of what your impending
decision would do to our wonderful island and home. This all being said, as
part of five generations on Salt Spring Island [1923], I would like to suggest
that the Club be allowed to exist with out the conditions that will surely
cause the Club to whither and die. As the CRD and the Club will never satisfy
Mr Milne with anything than a full shut down of the Club, I think it is time
for the CRD to stand up to Mr Milne and all his money. Take the lead from
an island institution and proud community member and just say NO to Mr Milne
and his payed supporters. Thank you for your time and consideration on this
very important community matter. If at any time you would like a hands on walk
about of the club to see first hand what has been done previously, recently and
in the future to reduce noise levels for our neighbours, please give me a call.

(the “Comments”)

[
5
]

These Comments, available for public viewing on
the CRD website, are said by the plaintiff to be defamatory. It should be noted
that Mr. Milne’s name was redacted from the published Comments. However, the
plaintiff alleges that an un-redacted version was distributed to members of the
CRD committee reviewing the noise by-law and to “a variety of people yet
unknown.”

[
6
]

The plaintiff commenced this action on November
14, 2014. At the time, Mr. Milne was unable to identify the author of the Comments
and named “John Doe” as a defendant. The CRD filed a response on December 10,
2014. The amended notice of civil claim was filed in February 2015 in which
Mr. McDonald is substituted for John Doe. Mr. McDonald filed his response the
month following.

[
7
]

The notice of application seeks an order that
either paragraph 17 a. - i. or, if not a., the remainder of those subparagraphs
be struck. The impugned pleading is:

17. In their natural and ordinary meaning,
or in the alternative by way of innuendo, the words of the Defamatory
Statements were meant, and understood to mean, that the plaintiff,
inter
alia:

a. commenced the Gun

Club Action and makes complaints to the CRD regarding the Gun Club for
ulterior motives;

b. manipulates,
bribes, or intimidates local government to achieve collateral goals;

c. files numerous
legal claims, particularly spurious legal claims, to put pressure on others and
to achieve collateral goals;

d. bribes
witnesses in legal proceedings in exchange for
favourable testimony;

e. is a criminal;

f. is a malingerer
and complainer;

g. is a habitual
or vexatious litigant;

h. filed the Gun
Club Action to:

i. put pressure on the Gun Club;

ii. cause the Gun Club to close; and

iii. cause the Gun
Club to sell its property so the plaintiff could purchase
the Gun Club lands at a discount, and develop them for profit; and

i. uses his personal resources to intimidate
others for his own

purposes.

[
8
]

On April 28, 2015, the defendant McDonald issued
a written demand for further particulars from the plaintiff pursuant to Rules
3-7(21)(a), (22) and (23) of the
SCCR.
A deadline for a response to the
demand was set for May 8, 2015 at 4 p.m. After initially rejecting the
request on legal principles, the plaintiff did provide some particulars by way
of a May 8, 2015 letter from counsel. Those particulars relate primarily to the
order sought in item 3 of the defendant McDonald’s application. The plaintiff
continues to resist the broader request for particulars.

The Law

A. Striking
pleadings

[
9
]

This aspect of the application mirrors the
relief sought in
Lund v. Black Press Group Ltd.,
2007 BCSC 559
. As the
court states in
Lund
:

[2]  Although the Defendants seek relief on
the basis of Rule 19(24)(a)-(d), I find that Rule 19(24)(a) is most applicable.
It reads as follows:

(24)  At any stage
of a proceeding the court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or
any part of an endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the ground
that

(a) it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,…

and the court may
grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed...

[3]  In
Citizens for Foreign Aid
Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4
th
)
266, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (B.C.S.C.) at para.
34
, Romilly J. provides a
concise summary of what is required to succeed on an application under Rule
19(24):

To succeed on an
application under Rule 19(24)(a) it must be established that it is "plain
and obvious" that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action:
Hunt v. Carey,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 (S.C.C.). If there is any doubt it should be
resolved in the favour of permitting the pleadings to stand: McGauley v.
British Columbia (1989),
1989 CanLII 2809 (BC CA)
, 39 B.C.L.R. (2d) 223 (B.C.C.A.). The court should
proceed on the assumption that all facts pled are true: Helman v. Brown (1966),

1966 CanLII 597 (BC CA)
, 57 W.W.R. 608 (B.C.C.A.). The only question then is whether the facts disclose
a cause of action: Minnes v. Minnes (1962),
1962 CanLII 350 (BC CA)
, 39 W.W.R. 112 (B.C.C.A.);
McNaughten v. Baker (1988),
1988 CanLII 3036 (BC CA)
, 25 B.C.L.R. (2d) 17 (C.A.). In other words, as long
as the pleadings disclose a triable issue, either as it exists, or as it may be
amended, then the issue should go to trial. The mere fact that the case is weak
or not likely to succeed is no ground for striking it out under the provisions
of Rule 19(24): Minnes, supra.

[4]  In determining whether it is plain and
obvious that defamation pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action, the
court will assess whether the words complained of are reasonably capable of
bearing the meanings alleged. In making such an assessment, the court will
determine whether reasonable persons of ordinary intelligence would read the
words complained of as lowering the plaintiff in the estimation of right
thinking members of society and cause him to be regarded with feelings of
hatred, contempt, ridicule, fear, dislike or disesteem (see
Sturdy v.
Canada (Minister of National Defence)
,

2005 BCSC 519
).

[5]  In the case at bar, the Defendants seek
only to strike select alleged meanings, not the entire defamation claims
against them. Although I was unable to find a B.C. case where a court
essentially pruned the pleadings in a defamation action, in my opinion there is
sufficient authority for doing so. First, Rule 19(24) states that a court may
strike out or amend the whole
or any part
of a pleading. I am satisfied
that the Rule provides authority to cull pleadings without striking the entire
claim. Indeed, under Rule 19(24), the court struck out only select phrases and
paragraphs of a statement of defence (see
Hemming v. Newton
,
2006
BCSC 1748
).

[6]  Second, the object of the
Rules of
Court
, as expressed in Rule 1(5) is to “secure the just, speedy and
inexpensive determination of every proceeding on its merits”. If the words
complained of in a defamation action are not reasonably capable of bearing some
of the meanings that are alleged, it would be efficient and just for the court
to strike those alleged meanings.

[7]  During submissions, counsel for the
plaintiff explained that he did not come prepared to argue whether or not the
Defendants’ statements are capable of bearing the meanings alleged. The
plaintiff submits that I must proceed on the premise that every fact alleged in
the Statement of Claim is true. In particular, the plaintiff submits that the
inferential meanings alleged must be presumed to be true. It is the plaintiff’s
position that whether words are capable of bearing the meanings alleged is more
properly argued under Rule 34. The plaintiff submits that the most the court
can do, on this application, is to order that certain statements and their
alleged meanings be set down for further argument on whether the words are
capable of bearing the meanings alleged.

[8]  I do not
agree with the plaintiff’s submissions. Whether words are capable of a
defamatory meaning is a question of law (
Lions Gate Marketing Company
Ltd. v. Used Car Dealers Association of Ontario
,
2005 BCCA 274
at para.

11
). Whether words actually mean what is alleged is a question of fact. The
only way that I can determine whether to strike any part of the pleadings in a
defamation case, pursuant to Rule 19(24), is to assess whether or not the words
are capable of supporting the meanings alleged. If I find, from the perspective
of a reasonable person of ordinary intelligence, that the words are not capable
of supporting the meanings alleged, I can strike them pursuant to Rule 19(24)
and do not have to set the matter over for consideration under Rule 34. In
deciding whether a plaintiff has disclosed a reasonable cause of action, I must
examine the legal basis for his claim. In defamation, this involves assessing
whether the allegedly defamatory words are capable of supporting the meanings
which are claimed.

[
10
]

Further, the court must “have regard to the meaning
which a reasonable person of ordinary intelligence would understand [the Comments]
given such a man’s general knowledge and experience in worldly affairs”:
Mitchell
v. Nanaimo District Teachers’ Assn.,
1994 CanLII 2593
(B.C.C.A.) at paras.

33 and 45
.

[
11
]

Nevertheless, the pleading will only be struck
in the “clearest of cases”:
Guergis v. Novak,
2013 ONCA 449
at para.
40
.

[
12
]

No evidence is admissible on this type of
application:
SCCR
9-5(2). A response to a demand for particulars is
incorporated into the NOCC such that the content of the May 8
th

letter from plaintiff’s counsel is merely an extension of the pleadings.

B. Particulars

[
13
]

As articulated in the defendant McDonald’s
notice of application,

in some cases, when a publication is reproduced
in its entirety in the pleadings, and numerous allegations of defamation are
derived from that publication, the plaintiff must provide particulars regarding
which portion of the publication is defamatory and in what way:
Thomas v.
McMullan,
2000 BCSC 863
. However, whether such particulars are necessary is
to be decided on a case by case basis. The objective of providing particulars
is to ensure that the opposing party knows the case to be met.

[
14
]

Rule 3-7(21)(a) governs this aspect of the
application. This sub-rule requires delivery of particulars only in situations
where the impugned words or statements could not be read as defamatory on a
literal meaning or by inference on their natural and ordinary meaning. Words or
statements can also be defamatory by virtue of extrinsic facts or circumstances
known only to the specific reader of the publication:
Reimer v. Dr. A.R.
Boyco Optometric Corporation,
2012 BCSC 860
at paras.
17-22
. In this last
situation, particulars of such facts or circumstances should be provided.

Discussion

[
15
]

It makes sense to first determine what portions
of the NOCC will stand before addressing whether particulars should be provided
on that pleading.

A. Striking
Pleadings

[
16
]

I find it to be plain and obvious that the
Comments are not capable of supporting the following meanings as pled in the
NOCC:

•

17 b. The plaintiff bribes or intimidates local
government to achieve collateral goals (but the allegation of manipulation can
stand);

•

17 e. The plaintiff is a criminal;

•

17 f. The plaintiff is a malingerer (but
allegation of complainer can stand).

[
17
]

The ordinary person might conclude that “using
the CRD” is equivalent to manipulation but the suggestion of bribery or intimidation
of local government is too far a stretch on the interpretation of, or inference
to be taken from, the language used in the Comments even including the
particulars provided with respect to “collateral goals.” Similarly, an ordinary
person would not infer from the Comments, even reading between the lines, that
Mr. Milne is a criminal. A malingerer is someone who feigns illness to avoid
work. There is nothing in the Comments which suggests even remotely that Mr.
Milne feigns illness let alone is seeking to avoid work.

[
18
]

On first reading, I might also have concluded
that paragraph 17 h. iii is incapable of being defamatory. However, the
particulars delivered by the plaintiff provide the additional facts which may
support the plea.

[
19
]

I am not so persuaded with respect to the balance
of the impugned pleas and any doubt must be resolved in favour of the pleading
standing for trial.

[
20
]

Thus, only those portions of the amended NOCC
identified in paragraph 16 above are struck.

B. Particulars

[
21
]

The next question is whether the plaintiff is
obliged to provide additional particulars on the pleading. Mr. McDonald’s
request for particulars is broken down between a specific and a more general
category. In the specific category, the applicant concedes that particulars
have been received on paragraphs 17 a., 17 b. and 17 c. of
the NOCC. Those particulars relate to the allegations of “ulterior motives” and
“collateral goals” as pled. The particulars also supplement the plea at
17 d., g. and h., although perhaps indirectly. In the general category,
the applicant still seeks particulars “regarding which portions of the alleged
defamatory comments pertain to each alleged defamatory meaning.”

[
22
]

In my view, Rule 3-7(21)(a) does not require the
plaintiff to effectively dissect the Comments and attribute certain words or
statements to each of the pleas found at paragraph 17 of the NOCC. Without
deciding the ultimate issue between the parties, the words contained in the
Comments could be defamatory on either a literal meaning of the words or by the
impression left by the statement as a whole. No additional extrinsic facts are
needed to illuminate or explain the defamatory nature of the Comments. Accordingly,
the relief sought in item 2 of the notice of application is dismissed.

[
23
]

In summary, paragraphs 17 b., e. and f. of the
NOCC are struck in part or on a whole as described. But for costs, the balance
of the relief sought is dismissed. Given the mixed result, costs of the
application will be in the cause as between the plaintiff and the defendant
McDonald.

“C.P.
Bouck”

Master
C.P. Bouck
